http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/03/trump.text: Iran's foreign ministry said on Monday there were currently no negotiations with the United States but talks were under way with Oman over the management of the Strait of Hormuz."We are not currently negotiating with the United States. Our negotiations are with Oman to secure passage through the Strait of Hormuz," said foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei during a weekly press briefing.That statement contradicts US President Donald Trump who said that new negotiations with Iran would begin on Monday after he decided to hold off on striking the Islamic republic to pursue a deal to end the war entering its sixth month.Trump told reporters on Sunday that the talks would cover the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies that has become a sticking point in the conflict, and the denuclearisation of Iran.For its part, Iran said it was nearing a deal with Oman over a new route through the strait, where a tanker reported an explosion nearby on Sunday, underscoring the continued volatility of the strategic waterway.Oil prices fell on Monday at the opening of Asian trade after Trump announced the new negotiations, with West Texas Intermediate dropping 4.7% to $80.72 (€69.99) per barrel.Washington and Tehran have been at war since 28 February, when the US and Israel launched surprise strikes against Iran, though months of on-off diplomacy have led to periods of relative calm.Following a return to strikes last month, fears had mounted that the fighting could escalate once again. Trump had threatened to hit Iran "very hard" and was reportedly considering renewed attacks including against energy infrastructure, with US embassies across the region on alert.Trump pulled back from that threat on Saturday, saying the "perimeters" of a deal were there."Now what we're doing is we're talking to them in the form of a negotiation. It begins tomorrow afternoon," Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One on Sunday, without providing details of the venue or participants in the talks.The US president said he had been asked by Iran as well as US partners Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar to hold off on the strikes, which he claimed would have been "the biggest attack since World War II."Iranian media denied that Tehran had asked Trump not to strike.A previous ceasefire deal that included the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz fell through and Iran has since tightened its control over the waterway.The US president said at the start of the conflict that the war was necessary to deal with Iran's nuclear programme. Western nations accuse Iran of seeking a bomb, though Tehran insists the programme is entirely civilian in nature.'Exchange of views'Iranian lawmaker Hassan Ghashghavi, spokesman for the parliament's national security commission, said on Sunday that mediators were trying to revive the US-Iran memorandum of understanding that was agreed in June.That agreement was not intended as a final peace deal, but as a stepping stone to negotiations on a comprehensive agreement, though it did include provisions on Hormuz."They know that the main issue and, in fact, the key to the matter right now is the issue of the Strait of Hormuz, so yes, there is an exchange of views," Ghashghavi said.Posting on X, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said: "We must strive to compel the enemy to remain committed to what it has signed."Deal with Oman?Before the war, there was free passage for all vessels through the Strait of Hormuz, but Iran closed the strait during the war and now insists on retaining control and charging tolls, something the US rejects.That dispute sparked the return to strikes last month, as Tehran refused to let ships travel any route other than one which hugs the Iranian coast.On Sunday, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei told state television that a deal was close with Oman, which sits on the other side of the strait, over a new route through it."We are now going to reach an understanding on a route acceptable to both sides, neither the northern route nor the southern route, but one that respects the sovereign rights of both sides and safeguards our national interests and security," he said.He insisted though that such an agreement did not mean the reopening of the strait.Maritime trade tracking firm Kpler said on Friday that traffic through Hormuz had dropped sharply.On Sunday, a tanker off the coast of Oman reported hearing an explosion near the vessel, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) Centre reported, adding that the vessel and crew were all safe.

https://www.dw.com/en/migrant-tunnels-in.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5ISMy Lithuanian authorities have discovered 12 border tunnels so far this year Image: Lithuania's State Border Guard Service Advertisement Migrants are taking a new route to enter the Baltic country Lithuania : underground tunnels. These could be yet another attempt by Belarus to foster political instability, experts say. The country's border guards say they have found 12 such tunnels since the beginning of the year near the Belarusian border, with a length of up to 25 meters on the Lithuanian side. They are expecting more to emerge. Lithuania's border with Belarus is about 700 kilometers long, around 550 kilometers of which are fenced. "We have a ground seismic system, which can detect easily when there's a high level of vibrations over a long period of time," General Rustamas Liubajevas, the commander of Lithuania's State Border Guard Service, explained to DW. "We then wait [outside a tunnel] for the final stage of the digging and when the migrants come out, we apprehend them," he said, adding that up to 40 migrants exiting such tunnels had been arrested. Last year Lithuania registered 1652 irregular border crossings Image: Lithuania's State Border Guard Service Lithuania's prosecutor's office confirmed to DW that a pre-trial investigation was under way concerning approximately 20 people suspected of illegally digging a tunnel. Possible charges also include people smuggling. Due to the investigation, no media visits are currently authorized at the sites. Liubajevas is surprised migrants would attempt a subterranean crossing. "It takes a lot of effort to dig a tunnel and the migrants are arrested almost immediately — at most, one small group gets through," he said. Is Minsk lending a hand? The elaborate nature of the tunnels has led him to believe the migrants aren't working alone. "They wouldn't be able to go through with this without logistical support from the Belarusian authorities, as they need a lot of material like wood to strengthen the tunnels' walls," he stressed, adding that Belarus seemingly wanted to "keep the level of tension at the border high." Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenkohas denied facilitating migration flows to neighboring states. Similar migrant tunnels were discovered in the past in neighboring Poland. Margarita Seselgyte, Director of the Institute of International Relations and Political Science at Vilnius University, seconded Liubajevas' view. "Belarus is watching its border very closely, and the country doesn't fit in the natural migration route of migrants from Afghanistan, Iran or Sri Lanka," she told DW, adding that Minsk had to at least have turned a blind eye to any digging activity taking place near the border. Some experts believe the Belarusian state is envouraging the building of tunnels across the border Image: Lithuania's State Border Guard Service Seselgyte thus sees the tunnels as "a hybrid attack to cause anxiety in our society." "There is no vacuum in the world of security. As Lithuania has been closing vulnerabilities and reinforcing its border fence, Belarus is now helping migrants pass beneath it," she said. A long-running issue at the eastern flank of Europe For her, Minsk is assisting its close ally Moscow . Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 partly from Belarus, where it amassed troops under the pretext of military drills. "Lithuania has been very vocal in terms of defense against Russia, both conventional and hybrid, on an EU and Nato level, and they want to silence that voice by causing chaos in our country," the political scientist said. "The main goal is probably to weaken support for Ukraine and disrupt European unity," she added. Linas Kojala, CEO of Vilnius-based think tank Geopolitics and Security Studies Center, noted that the tunnels were keeping the border force busy – even if only a few migrants got through. He described the tunnels as "just another phase of the attack of weaponized migration we've been facing since 2021." Most of the Lithuania-Belarus border is lined with fencing Image: Arnaud Dumontier/MAXPPP/IMAGO That's when tens of thousands of migrants crossed into Lithuania, Poland and Latvia from Belarus. The European Union called the events a "state-sponsored instrumentalization of migrants at the EU external border," organized by Lukashenko. "Latvia, Poland, Lithuania and other countries have since set up external borders and we've managed to bring down illegal migration to a minimum," Kojala told DW. Lithuania's border guards registered 1652 attempts to enter the country irregularly in 2025. But this number won't go down to zero unless Minsk deals with the problem on its side, according to Kojala. "And that's unlikely: Belarus is clearly trying to pose as many problems as possible." 'Migration has long been used as a strategic tool' Belarus would be far from the first country to use migration as a strategic tool, underlined Robert Gonzci, an analyst at the Migration Research Institute in the Hungarian capital of Budapest. "It's a relatively low-cost, low-risk way of exerting pressure on other countries, and since the 1950s, there've been numerous documented cases of governments creating or manipulating migration flows," he said to DW. He added that even the Assyrian empire – which collapsed in the seventh century BC – used migration to consolidate imperial control. Gonzci didn't rule out that autonomous smuggling networks might be behind the recently discovered tunnels, which Belarusian authorities don't fully control. He added that Belarus and Russia have used weaponized migration to "divert Western attention from Russia's broader strategic agenda and create instability along NATO's eastern flank by fueling political and social tensions within European countries." Poland's EU border: A threat to nature and people To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The states organizing such operations – often authoritarian regimes – enjoyed an inherent strategic advantage, Gonzci stressed. "The target is usually a democratic state facing a fundamental dilemma: They must protect their sovereignty by securing their borders while simultaneously upholding their legal obligations and humanitarian commitments," he said. Eastern countries 'showing resilience' But experts seem to agree that countries on the EU's eastern flank have been doing rather well in that respect. "There's increasing cooperation and coordination between the Nordic and Baltic States and Poland, as these countries are facing similar challenges. And the EU Frontex mission has been sending additional equipment," Seselgyte said. Lithuania is currently receiving technical support from neighboring countries. "We are testing Polish scanning equipment, through which we can identify empty spaces underground. If these tools work well, we'll buy and deploy them," explained Liubajevas. https://www.dw.com/en/heat-wave-threaten.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5HrGE French authorities worked to keep vacationers away around Bordeaux, banning holiday camps for children and for people with disabilities Image: Emma Da Silva/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement A forecast of an incoming heat wave across France and Spain this week is threatening to hamper firefighting efforts as some of Europe's worst wildfires in decades rage on. France's weather service forecast temperatures of up to 40 degrees Celsius (100 degrees Fahrenheit) from Tuesday, while Spain's AEMET warned of a new heat wave from Wednesday till the end of the week, with highs of 42 degree Celsius in the northeast and 39 degrees Celsius in central regions. Authorities said soaring temperatures, dry winds and low humidity would push wildfire danger to "extreme" levels, even as forests turned tinder-dry by successive heat waves this year. The return of searing temperatures, from Tuesday in France and from Wednesday in Spain, threaten to complicate fire-fighting efforts [FILE: July 23, 2026] Image: Julien De Rosa/AFP Thousands of firefighters and water-dropping aircraft raced to contain the blazes before temperatures rise further. Experts linked the scale of the fires to increasingly frequent and intense heat waves driven by climate change , as hotter and drier conditions are making wildfires more destructive. Macron warns of 'hard' times In France, President Emmanuel Macron said one fire in the Landes region had been contained, but a much larger wildfire near Bordeaux continued to burn after scorching about 42,000 hectares, forcing around 220,000 people to evacuate and destroying hundreds of homes. "The weeks ahead will be hard. We must hold firm," Macron said. Overnight on Tuesday, firefighters prevented a massive wildfire along the Atlantic coast west of Bordeaux from spreading, authorities said. According to officials, 93 firefighters have been injured since the operation began. Aid from Germany arrived in the region on Monday in the form of two transport helicopters and an A400M transport aircraft carrying equipment. In Spain, wildfires west of Madrid and in other regions have forced about 60,000 people to flee. With the coming heat wave threatening to fuel further spread of the wildfires, Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska firefighters in Spain made progress after a "positive night" against wildfires to the west of Madrid. Some 150,000 hectares of land have burned in Spain and 115,000 hectares in France since the start of this year. At a campsite near Navaluenga, west of the capital, ravaged by Spain's worst wildfire on record, the site co-owner Maria Angeles Canete said her family lost everything. "We had this campsite, we had another one, and we've lost it all. We have nothing," she told the AFP news agency. Has Europe lost control of its wildfires? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video EU firefighting resources stretched thin The European Union deployed additional firefighting aircraft to France, while EU commissioner Hadja Lahbib warned that resources are under growing strain as extreme fire conditions spread across southern and central Europe. "Extreme conditions are looming for Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic, in addition to France, the Iberian Peninsula... where the situation is expected to worsen, including in Portugal starting today," Lahbib said. In Italy , a wildfire in the southern Puglia region forced the evacuation of hundreds of tourists from beaches and campgrounds, authorities said. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/c74emd.text: Orangutans in danger as wildfires blaze through Borneo Orangutans in danger as wildfires blaze through Borneo Close A weak orangutan was found laying on the ground in Ketapang, West Kalimantan on Borneo island. Indonesia has intensified efforts to contain haze from wildfires across six provinces in Borneo and Sumatra islands. The wildfires have destroyed part of the habitat of hundreds of orangutans and risking the survival of the species. "The situation is quite critical", said Karmele Llano Sanchez, CEO of the wildlife foundation Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI). Sanchez said the fires are "leaving [the orangutans] without any food or water". The orangutan found will be moved to a rehabilitation centre to get more treatment and will be released back into the wild after recovery, according to YIARI. The transaction, which closed on 30 September 2026, marks the group’s entry into the Romanian market and represents its first acquisition since becoming part of Axcel’s portfolio in 2025. Wolf Theiss advised Nordic Tyre Group on the Romanian law aspects of the transaction, including assistance with due diligence, transaction structuring and the transfer of the entire share capital of Dinamic92 Distribution S.R.L. as well as coordination with the client and other advisors involved in the transaction. The Wolf Theiss team was led by Partner Ileana Glodeanu, supported by Senior Associate Delia Dumitrescu and Associates Vlad Catană and Laurenţiu Bolborici (all Corporate/M&A). The team further included Counsel Flavius Florea (Data Protection, IP & TMT), Partner Anca Jurcovan, Senior Associate Maria Popescu (both Competition & FDI), Partner Adelina Iftime-Blăgean, Counsel Andreea Stan (both Employment), Senior Associate Smaranda Văcaru (Banking & Finance), Counsel Dana Toma, Senior Associate Antonia Nica and Associate Sorana Grosu (all Real Estate & Construction) and Senior Associate Bogdan Lamatic (Litigation). “ Nordic Tyre Group’s entry into Romania with Dinamic92 represents a strategic expansion into Eastern Europe and marks the next growth chapter for the group. We appreciate the support of the Wolf Theiss throughout the signing and closing of our acquisition in Romania. Ileana and the entire team understood our objectives and helped bring the transaction to a successful close.” – Patrick Bergander, CEO, Nordic Tyre Group “It was a pleasure to support Nordic Tyre on this transaction and its entry into the Romanian market. We would like to thank all parties involved for their collaboration throughout the process, we are very happy to have contributed to the successful completion of this acquisition.” – Ileana Glodeanu, M&A Partner, Wolf Theiss Nordic Tyre Group is one of the leading independent tyre wholesale and distribution platforms in Europe, operating across the Nordics and Baltics, with annual revenue of approximately EUR 400 million. The group is backed by Nordic private equity firm Axcel and combines a strong supplier network, extensive logistics setup, and a unique, proprietary software platform to provide the broadest and most reliable tyre offering to its customers. Dinamic92 Distribution is the leading independent tyre wholesaler in Romania. Founded in 1992 by the Tofan family in Piatra Neamt, the company has grown over more than three decades into a trusted partner for tyre retailers and workshops across the country. Dinamic92 serves a wide range of customers, from independent workshops to national tyre retailers, through locations in Piatra Neamţ, Cluj-Napoca, Constanţa, Timişoara and Bucharest, with an annual distribution volume of approximately 700,000 tyres. Ukraine: Russian drone attacks hit Kyiv hospital, leave two dead in Odesa Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 13 November 2026 - 12:00 GMT+1 Russian overnight attacks on Ukraine killed at least two person in Odesa and injured another at a hospital in Kyiv. Rescuers evacuated patients, including people using wheelchairs and crutches, as firefighters battled the flames. … More In the capital's Shevchenkivskyi district, a strike sparked a fire at a medical facility and partially destroyed its second floor , Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported. Hospital staff evacuated 30 people , while emergency crews rescued another seven. Footage released by the emergency service shows patients being helped to safety, including people using wheelchairs and crutches, as firefighters work to extinguish the blaze. Other images reveal damaged windows, smoke rising from the building and rescue workers moving through hospital corridors. The fire had been extinguished. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT In the southern port city of Odesa, a separate Russian drone attack killed two people and injured five others, according to Serhii Lysak, head of the city's military administration. A private house and several vehicles were also damaged in the strikes, while nighttime footage shows firefighters tackling a blaze at the scene. The attacks affected two major Ukrainian cities , with emergency services responding to fires, damaged buildings and casualties. In Kyiv, the evacuation of patients highlighted the disruption caused when medical facilities are struck, particularly for people with reduced mobility. The incidents come as Russia continues its aerial attacks on Ukraine more than four years after launching its full-scale invasion in February 2022 . https://www.dw.com/en/czech-arms-makers-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5P9P9 Prefer DW on Google Russia's war in Ukraine has driven major growth across the Czech defense industry as a whole Image: Dalibor Gluck/CTK Photo/IMAGO Advertisement The Czechoslovak Group (CSG) arms maker announced in mid-October that it has acquired a stake in Canadian space technology manufacturer MDA Space. This space mission is part of the company's bid to continue riding the boom that has transformed its fortunes in recent years. When it listed on the Amsterdam Stock Exchange earlier this year, CSG soared to become the most valuable company in Central and Eastern Europe, with a market capitalization of €14.6 billion ($16.4 billion), propelling its owner, Michal Strnad, to the top of the region's rich list. From 90s startup to major European player CSG began life as a 1990s startup , selling military surplus amid the collapse of the Warsaw Pact, the military alliance between the Soviet Union and Europe's socialist Eastern Bloc nations, which was founded in 1955 and disbanded in 1991. When it listed on the Amsterdam Stock Exchange earlier this year, CSG became the most valuable company in Central and Eastern Europe. Pictured here: CSG chairman and owner Michal Strnad Image: Jan Lopatka/REUTERS It has since grown to become the second-largest producer of ammunition in Europe after Germany's Rheinmetall and now produces across Europe and in the US . The impact of the war in Ukraine The main driver of the company's rising fortunes has been Russia's war in Ukraine , which has driven a dramatic boom across the Czech defense industry as a whole. In 2021, the sector's exports totaled €600 million. In 2025, these exports had expanded to €4.7 billion, powered by orders placed by Kyiv and its European allies. By the end of that year, European states had procured approximately €11 billion worth of military support for Ukraine from Czech defense firms. Orders to the value of roughly €4 billion have arrived via the Czech Ammunition Initiative, a program that coordinates the transfer of artillery shells to Ukraine. While drones play a major role in the war in Ukraine, both sides continue to attack each other with artillery fire Image: Jose Colon/Anadolu/picture alliance Amid the avalanche of orders sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, CSG and Czech peers such as STV, Colt CZ and PBS have been busy expanding production to pump out military vehicles and planes, guns, grenades, shells and bullets. Historical link "The war in Ukraine, particularly in its early stages, was especially well suited to Czech firms," Krzysytof Debiec of the Centre for Eastern Studies (OSW) told DW. Debiec says that this was largely due to the major role that the former Czechoslovakia played in supplying Warsaw Pact countries. "Specialization in the production of ammunition — including Soviet calibers — the repair of Soviet-era equipment and the manufacture of relatively unsophisticated systems that could be rapidly introduced and were compatible with the Ukrainian army's existing stocks," have all been key, he explained. At the same time, European states eyeing the threat from the east and broader geopolitical instability are boosting their own defense budgets. "The shift in US policies vis-a-vis NATO is forcing European nations to increase their defense spending dramatically, and that's another factor" in the Czech defense industry boom, Jan Jires, a former deputy defense minister and now a senior advisor at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, told DW. Export dependence However, since launching on the stock exchange, CSG's share price has performed erratically, illustrating the shifting sands on which Czechia 's booming defense industry now stands. The populist ruling coalition under Prime Minister Andrej Babis (pictured here) is divided on the issue of support for Ukraine Image: Beata Zawrzel/ZUMA/IMAGO The government in Prague has responded to the sector's surge by transferring the defense industry portfolio from the Ministry of Defense to the Ministry of Industry and Trade to align its growing role in exports with national economic and trade policy. At the same time, the populist ruling coalition that took power a year ago is made up of parties that have either promised to lower support for Ukraine or — in the case of the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy party (SPD) — are openly pro-Russian. As a result, the coalition has halted contributions to the Czech Ammunition Initiative and is dragging its feet on raising defense spending to meet NATO targets . This only limits an already small domestic market, leaving the industry dependent on exports for about 90% of its revenue — the vast bulk of which is still linked to Ukraine — and lacking a stable base for expansion. "The Czech industry has outgrown the country's financial means," said Jires. "Unlike German, French or British companies, Czech manufacturers cannot rely on domestic demand to make them globally relevant." What the future holds Increased global defense spending looks set to continue, but an end to Russia's war in Ukraine, a change in US foreign policy or a calmer geopolitical environment would hit Czech arms manufacturers hard. For this reason, they must ponder what the future of war, and its funding, might look like. The US has repeatedly said that it expects its European allies in NATO to increase defense spending Image: Stoyan Nenov/REUTERS The conflict in Ukraine offers some indicators, having become increasingly focused on swarms of drones and a technological race between Kyiv and Moscow to improve the performance of the unmanned aircraft. Major questions must now be asked regarding "the size and role of the military, how it is equipped, what should be purchased and when new weaponry can arrive" Andor Sandor, a defense analyst and former commander of Czechia's Military Intelligence Service, told DW. For a company like CSG, for which bullets and shells currently account for around 60% of sales, these are vital questions. "Czech companies — many of which still focus on relatively unsophisticated military production — must invest more in innovative manufacturing," said Debiec, who notes that most are well aware of the challenge. "They have reinvested their extraordinary profits and are already more technologically advanced and diversified in their production than they were in 2022." Space mission CSG's acquisition of MDA Space is part of such efforts. Most Czech defense companies are already more technologically advanced and diversified than they were when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 Image: Eva Korinkova/REUTERS The company, which already held interests in British and German space technology companies, pointed to the close link between the space and defense industries when it announced the deal. Noting that global government spending on space defense accelerated to €65.83 billion last year, CSG estimates that the overall space economy will triple in size to €1.6 trillion over the next decade. Developing capabilities in space is "a natural extension" of its activities, the company stated, noting plans for further development in the segment, including a "dedicated space team." To power such missions, Czech defense companies must make sure they're in a position to tap into funds for defense and space under the next EU budget, which could rise as high as €130 billion, said Jires. "If they fail to do so, and all this money is grabbed by German, French and Italian companies," he warned, "Czech manufacturers may miss the opportunity to truly scale-up." https://www.politico.eu/article/european.text: BERLIN — The proposal from U.S. President Donald Trump’s negotiating team to give Ukraine a NATO-style collective defense guarantee has triggered an unusual new mindset among some of Kyiv’s allies in Europe: optimism. European officials close to the peace negotiations are cautiously hopeful that the offer could signal a shift in America’s position in Ukraine’s favor — even though they remain wary that the price Trump will demand for such a sweeping commitment could be too high. After two weeks of shuttle diplomacy, Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner proposed the security guarantee at last week’s press conference in Berlin, claiming the U.S. president is “open” to such a “big deal” and the Russians are now “comfortable” with it too. Advertisement Advertisement Neither is yet certain, and one Russian official dismissed the idea. But Russian President Vladimir Putin himself has not yet publicly rejected Kushner’s plan, and European negotiators are taking it seriously, even if they want more information about how it would work. A security guarantee for Ukraine based on NATO’s Article 5 collective defense clause, which states that an attack on one member shall be treated as an attack on all, would change the game when it comes to deterring Russia from invading Ukraine again after this war ends. That is particularly true if, as implied, America, with its mighty military, is bound into such a guarantee. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, French President Emmanuel Macron, US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff, back, and U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner leave a Coalition of the Willing media call in Berlin on Nov. 19, 2026. | Pool photo by Hannah McKay/Getty Images While few details are known about the proposal, it would, if backed up by robust legal, military and political commitments, mean that a new attack on Ukraine would risk a direct conflict with the U.S. An aide in French President Emmanuel Macron’s office said the U.S. is heading in “the right direction” but called on the White House to go a step further and give Ukraine full NATO membership. An Article 5 guarantee “is obviously the best guarantee of solidarity among allies,” said the aide, who, like others, was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “So, if we say we’re giving Ukraine Article 5-type guarantees, we shouldn’t overcomplicate things: It means that Ukraine is joining NATO. The alliance’s credibility rests above all on Article 5. Article 5 is an article of faith.” Advertisement Advertisement Shifting the mood One reason why some Europeans believe Kushner’s offer is a genuine one is that he was not speaking off the cuff. In private, U.S. officials have been floating the idea for months. There has even been discussion behind the scenes of the French proposal for full NATO membership. Although Ukraine joining NATO is seen as a red line issue Russia would never agree to, Kushner and co. clearly believe their efforts to discuss an Article 5-like option with the Russians have found support in Moscow. And the mood in some parts of Europe has shifted as a result. Families shelter overnight at a Kyiv metro station following warnings of possible Russian air attacks late on Nov. 19, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. | Roman Pilipey/AFP via Getty Images Diplomats and officials who have spent much of the past two years of Trump’s second term despairing about his repeated torchings of the Western alliance — and worrying that he will sell out Ukraine — now sound relaxed about the U.S. “Clear progress has been made on security guarantees,” said one European official close to the negotiations. “On peace talks there is alignment with the U.S., no maximalist demands and no discussion on European security without the Europeans.” The aim now is that more progress will be possible toward targeted ceasefires in the energy sector and the Black Sea the next time the U.S. convenes peace talks between Russia and Ukraine, not least because Europeans will have their places at the negotiating table. That meeting is yet to be scheduled but officials expect it to take place in Abu Dhabi sometime after the American Thanksgiving holiday on Nov. 26. Advertisement Advertisement Details matter Not everyone is convinced. Speaking after Kushner’s announcement, Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was “not sure” everyone had the same understanding of what an Article 5-like guarantee would mean. “What does it mean, Article 5? That there are some forces of partners on your land. So, my question is: What about American soldiers?” He said Ukraine “would be happy” if the U.S. put military bases in the country “like in the Middle East.” Other Europeans agreed that there was still a lack of detail about exactly what Kushner’s plan would involve. People walk across a bridge during a blackout in Kyiv caused by attacks on Ukraine’s energy facilities on Nov. 20, 2026. | Genya Savilov/AFP via Getty Images The most skeptical Europeans are to be found in countries that share borders and a history with Russia, such as Poland and the Nordic and Baltic states, which are often the most hawkish toward Moscow. Poland will be part of the official European negotiating team, which is expected to join the next round of direct negotiations between Russia, the U.S. and Ukraine. One risk Europeans are alive to is that the cost of such a security guarantee could prove to be too high. Americans asked Ukraine recently whether it would give Russia the whole of Donbas in exchange for full NATO membership. That would mean handing over land to Putin that he has not managed to win by fighting. Keeping Russia happy Ukraine’s territory is not the only issue on the table in these negotiations. Kushner has been equally insistent that revising the entire security framework that had governed Europe before the war is essential, including NATO’s relations with Russia. His broad argument is that if Europe’s security framework had been working properly, the war would never have happened. Advertisement Advertisement Among Ukraine’s more than 35 allies who gathered in Berlin for the Coalition of the Willing meeting last week, some see Kushner’s point. That’s why the EU’s institutions are happy to offer Putin the chance to discuss European security in a “parallel” track with a peace deal for Ukraine. To other more hawkish officials, Kushner’s argument about overhauling the continent’s defense framework still sounds dangerously like Putin speaking. They comfort themselves with the thought that no decisions will be taken without Europe “at the table” — but being present doesn’t necessarily equate to being in control. “The danger is that an Article 5-style guarantee could somehow become a Trojan Horse in the case of a wider bargain with Moscow, in which Ukraine would surrender the Donbas and ⁠NATO would accept restrictions on its military presence in Eastern Europe,” said Grégoire Roos, of London’s Chatham House think tank. Russia’s President Vladimir Putin, China’s President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump meet in Shenzen, China, on Nov. 19, 2026. | Pool picture by Andres Martinez Casares/Getty Images “Let’s face it: That would basically give Russia a de facto veto over European security. So, yes, we could potentially end up offering Ukraine the vague promise of collective defence while sapping the basic conditions that would actually make it credible.” Roos said he did not believe the Europeans would fall for such a trap. In Poland, for example, officials are watchful for traps and remain steadfast in backing Ukraine, he said. Trump’s friends Timing is also a factor that could be decisive. A European official said Trump wants a deal within weeks — even by the time he hosts G20 leaders in Florida in mid-December, though that won’t happen. Zelenskyy told reporters on Saturday that Americans “really wanted to get all this done before Christmas.” Another key deadline could be Jan. 3, when the new Democratic-controlled Congress starts work. Advertisement Advertisement Some leaders who met with Kushner and Witkoff in Berlin last week had feared Washington would be exerting much more pressure for a deal by the end of the year, according to one person present. But in the end leaders were relieved that the U.S. was not strong-arming Ukraine and its allies to rush to an agreement, the person said. Then there is the influence of another key group to keep in mind: Trump’s friends. While EU diplomats voiced relief that the summit in Shenzhen between Trump, Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping did not deliver a worse outcome for Ukraine and Europe, it still resulted in a joint “peace” declaration in which the trio pledged to reform the United Nations, slapped down the International Criminal Court, and promised to keep talking among themselves about nuclear arms. Trump doubled down on the value of having a close relationship with his “friend” Putin in a press conference on his return to Washington on Friday. “He’d love to end the war,” Trump said of the Russian leader — on the same day that two Russian missiles and a drone hit Poland, and Danish police announced they had thwarted a Russian plot to assassinate a Ukrainian rapper. The China summit serves as a reminder to European optimists that whatever they discuss with Kushner and Witkoff in Berlin or Abu Dhabi, ultimately only one person will make the key decisions for the U.S. — and Putin’s line into him just got stronger. “A precedent was created,” said another European official involved in recent diplomacy. “It wasn’t great.” Clea Caulcutt contributed reporting from Paris.
